title: Report on Studying Abroad at Tulane / Freiburg University
paragraphs: From the end of March 2012, I was given the opportunity to do clinical clerkships for two months at Tulane University in the United States and for one month at Freiburg University in Germany. The main reason I aspired to this study abroad was that I wanted to acquire a more objective way of seeing things by going outside Japan and actually seeing the medical care of various countries with my own eyes. By comparing the medical care of Japan, America and Germany, I would become able to look at Japanese medical care from a more objective viewpoint. With that in mind, I took on the clerkships in America and Germany.

In my first month at Tulane University I rotated through neurology. The first job I was given was following up on the patients I was in charge of. However, while the students on the same team gave splendid presentations, I could not even finish writing the chart in time. Telling myself that from here there was nothing but growth, I faced the clerkship from the next day. I received advice every time from the students on the same team, my presentations became passable, and the things I could do gradually increased. It was a month in which I felt myself growing every day. In the second month, in endocrinology, I was able to get through the clerkship far more smoothly than in the first month.

What was especially impressive in the American clerkship was the difference in practical ability between Japanese students and American students. Because the educational policies of Japan and America are different, Japanese students are strong in detailed knowledge of individual diseases, whereas in the practical ability to assess and plan for patients, I thought American students were overwhelmingly more capable. Regarding education too, I thought the system in which a student can do the first-touch examination and afterwards receive double and triple feedback from residents, fellows, attendings and others was very attractive. I thought that practical knowledge accumulates from this kind of practical education. I felt that this is an attitude we should adopt in Japan too, taking in whatever can be taken in.

At Freiburg University, I trained for one month on the pediatric oncology team. Since I do not speak German, it was mainly a shadowing style in which I followed behind the doctors. For individual patients I was given a brief history in English, so the style was to keep asking the doctors about whatever I wanted to hear. I also observed many procedures such as bone marrow aspiration and lumbar puncture. In addition, I observed a blood coagulation disorder clinic under Dr. 中村, who is currently working in Freiburg, and was taught how to look at blood specimens by Dr. 吉見 of Nagoya University, who works at the MDS study center.

The clerkship in Germany was different again from that in America. Compared with the American clerkship, it was rather close to the Japanese clerkship, and I think it tested one's initiative. For me, who cannot speak German, it was necessary to cut in in English among doctors conversing in German, so it was a clerkship that demanded more proactiveness than in America. What was impressive during the clerkship was that a considerable number of patients had come from other countries specially to receive German medical care. I realised that German medical care is still advanced within Europe. I was able to learn a great deal in this clerkship too, but I would like to visit Germany again after learning German once more.

By studying abroad in America and Germany this time, I think I was able to notice many things that I would not have noticed, because they would have seemed obvious, if I had stayed in Japan. Of course, three months is a short period and has its limits, but I think my horizons broadened greatly through studying abroad, and I was able to acquire a more objective way of seeing things for thinking about the future of Japanese medical care.

I would like to express my heartfelt thanks to the doctors of the International Exchange Office, the academic affairs staff, the local doctors who gave me this wonderful opportunity, the doctors and seniors who instructed me in the pre-departure training, and all my classmates who encouraged one another during the study abroad. Thank you very much indeed.
